text: God helps those who help themselves.
explanation: Originated in Aesop's Fables and popularized by Benjamin Franklin in Poor Richard's Almanack (1736). Scripture actually teaches God helps the helpless.
misconception: Widely assumed to be a proverb of Solomon.

text: Cleanliness is next to godliness.
explanation: Coined by Methodist founder John Wesley in an 1778 sermon on dress.
misconception: Sounds like an Old Testament Levitical purification rule.

text: This too shall pass.
explanation: A medieval Persian adage popularized in English by Edward FitzGerald and Abraham Lincoln.

text: Money is the root of all evil.
explanation: 1 Timothy 6:10 states: 'The LOVE of money is a root of all kinds of evil.' Money itself is not evil.
misconception: Dropping 'the love of' radically alters the meaning.

text: Spare the rod, spoil the child.
explanation: From Samuel Butler's 1664 poem Hudibras. Proverbs 13:24 says: 'Whoever spares the rod hates his son.'
misconception: A popular rhyming couplet substituting for scripture.

text: God will not give you more than you can handle.
explanation: A distortion of 1 Corinthians 10:13, which speaks of temptation, not life burdens. Paul wrote he was burdened beyond his ability to endure (2 Cor 1:8).
misconception: Frequently offered as comfort during grief.

text: Pride comes before a fall.
explanation: Proverbs 16:18 says: 'Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.'
misconception: The biblical text says 'haughty spirit before a fall'.

text: Love the sinner, hate the sin.
explanation: Originated in a letter by Saint Augustine (424 AD) and later popularized by Mahatma Gandhi.
misconception: Many assume this is a quote from Jesus Christ.

text: Three wise men visited the baby Jesus in the manger.
explanation: Matthew 2 mentions magi from the east with three gifts (gold, frankincense, myrrh), but never gives their number, and they visited a house, not a stable.
misconception: Nativity pageants combined the shepherds and three gifts.

text: Eve ate an apple from the forbidden tree.
explanation: Genesis 3:6 says only 'fruit'. The apple tradition arose from the Latin pun on 'malus' (evil/apple) and Milton's Paradise Lost.
misconception: Latin wordplay led Western art to portray an apple.

text: The lion shall lay down with the lamb.
explanation: Isaiah 11:6 actually says: 'The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat.'
misconception: A prominent example of cultural Mandela effect.

text: To thine own self be true.
explanation: Spoken by Polonius in William Shakespeare's play Hamlet (Act 1, Scene 3).
misconception: Frequently cited as biblical advice for integrity.

text: Charity begins at home.
explanation: Coined by Sir Thomas Browne in 1642, echoing Roman playwright Terence.
misconception: Sounds like New Testament pastoral advice.

text: A fool and his money are soon parted.
explanation: Written by English poet Thomas Tusser in 'Five Hundred Points of Good Husbandry' (1573).
misconception: Often presumed to be from Proverbs.

text: Hell hath no fury like a woman scorned.
explanation: Written by playwright William Congreve in The Mourning Bride (1697).

text: Every cloud has a silver lining.
explanation: Coined by John Milton in his 1634 masque Comus.
misconception: Quoted in devotional contexts as scripture.

text: The eye is the window to the soul.
explanation: An ancient proverb traced to Cicero. Matthew 6:22 says the eye is the lamp of the body.
misconception: Often conflated with Jesus's teaching on the eye.

text: Practice what you preach.
explanation: An English proverb from the 17th century. Matthew 23:3 touches on hypocrisy, but does not use this idiom.

text: When God closes a door, he opens a window.
explanation: Popularized in the 1965 musical The Sound of Music.

text: Jonah was swallowed by a whale.
explanation: Jonah 1:17 says the Lord prepared a 'great fish' (Hebrew: dag gadol).
misconception: Popular children's retellings specify a whale.

text: God bless this mess.
explanation: A 20th-century American home decor expression, not biblical text.

text: Everything happens for a reason.
explanation: A popular philosophical fatalism often confused with Romans 8:28.
misconception: Romans 8:28 promises God works all things together for good, not fatalism.

text: The Seven Deadly Sins.
explanation: Formulated by Pope Gregory the Great in 590 AD and systematized by Thomas Aquinas; never listed as a collective group in scripture.
misconception: Commonly thought to be a chapter in the Bible.

text: Halo over an angel's head.
explanation: Derived from Greek and Roman solar iconography and medieval Byzantine iconography.
misconception: Angelic descriptions in the Bible do not mention halos.

text: Satan rules as king in hell with a pitchfork.
explanation: Heavily influenced by Dante's Inferno, Milton's Paradise Lost, and Greek god Pluto/Hades.
misconception: The Bible describes hell as a place of punishment for Satan, not his throne.

text: Holy Moses!
explanation: An 18th-century American minced oath, not from the Bible.
misconception: American slang invoking a biblical character.

text: Give a man a fish, feed him for a day; teach a man to fish, feed him for a lifetime.
explanation: A 19th-century English proverb written by novelist Anne Isabella Thackeray Ritchie.
misconception: Frequently attributed to Jesus or Chinese philosophy.

text: A rolling stone gathers no moss.
explanation: First recorded in Latin by Publilius Syrus and Erasmus.
misconception: Sounds like a proverb of Solomon.

text: Birds of a feather flock together.
explanation: First recorded in English by William Turner in The Rescuing of Romish Fox (1545).

text: Honesty is the best policy.
explanation: Coined by Sir Edwin Sandys in 1599 and popularized by Benjamin Franklin.
misconception: Thought to be an Old Testament proverb.

text: Look before you leap.
explanation: Traced to Aesop's fable of The Fox and the Goat.

text: Time heals all wounds.
explanation: Attributed to ancient Greek poet Menander and Roman poet Ovid.

text: Silence is golden.
explanation: From an ancient Arabic and German proverb popularized by Thomas Carlyle in 1831.
misconception: Sounds like Proverbs 17:28 on holding one's tongue.

text: All that glitters is not gold.
explanation: From William Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice (Act 2, Scene 7).
misconception: Often thought to be in Proverbs.

text: Two wrongs don't make a right.
explanation: Recorded in English letters in 1734. Romans 12:17 says 'repay no one evil for evil.'
misconception: Folk phrasing of a biblical principle.

text: Where there's a will, there's a way.
explanation: An English proverb dating back to George Herbert's 1640 collection.

text: Better late than never.
explanation: Traced to Geoffrey Chaucer in The Yeoman's Tale (c. 1386).

text: Actions speak louder than words.
explanation: First recorded in English in 1736 by Thomas Fraser.
misconception: Parallels 1 John 3:18, but the exact idiom is English.

text: Laughter is the best medicine.
explanation: Proverbs 17:22 says: 'A merry heart does good, like medicine.' The modern idiom was popularized by Reader's Digest.

text: The grass is always greener on the other side.
explanation: A 20th-century American song and folk idiom.

text: Beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
explanation: Coined by Irish author Margaret Wolfe Hungerford in 1878.
misconception: Assumed to be in Song of Solomon.

text: Patience is a virtue.
explanation: From William Langland's Piers Plowman (c. 1377). Galatians 5:22 lists patience as a fruit of the Spirit, but not this phrase.

text: Rome was not built in a day.
explanation: A French medieval proverb recorded in 1190 AD.

text: Blood is thicker than water.
explanation: First recorded in medieval German in Reynard the Fox (1180).

text: Knowledge is power.
explanation: Coined by English philosopher Sir Francis Bacon in Meditationes Sacrae (1597).
misconception: Sounds like Proverbs 24:5 ('a man of knowledge increases strength').

text: An eye for an eye will make the whole world blind.
explanation: Commonly attributed to Mahatma Gandhi in the 20th century.
misconception: Critique of the lex talionis in Exodus 21:24.

text: Curiosity killed the cat.
explanation: Originally 'Care killed the cat' in Ben Jonson's 1598 play Every Man in His Humour.

text: Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
explanation: From Aesop's fable of The Milkmaid and Her Pail.

text: You can't teach an old dog new tricks.
explanation: From John Fitzherbert's The Boke of Husbandry (1534).

text: The apple doesn't fall far from the tree.
explanation: First noted in German by Ralph Waldo Emerson in 1839.

text: Too many cooks spoil the broth.
explanation: Recorded in English in 1575 by George Gascoigne.

text: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
explanation: Traced to Hugh Rhodes in 1530 and medieval Latin proverbs.

text: What goes around comes around.
explanation: An American idiom originating in the 1960s.

text: The pen is mightier than the sword.
explanation: Coined by English author Edward Bulwer-Lytton in 1839.

text: Beggar can't be choosers.
explanation: Recorded in John Heywood's 1546 proverb collection.

text: Easy come, easy go.
explanation: Recorded in John Heywood's 1546 dialogue of proverbs.

text: Kill two birds with one stone.
explanation: From Thomas Hobbes's 1656 work on liberty and necessity.

text: Ignorance is bliss.
explanation: From Thomas Gray's 1742 poem Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College.

text: Good things come to those who wait.
explanation: From Violet Fane's 1892 poem Tout vient à qui sait attendre.

text: A penny saved is a penny earned.
explanation: Coined by Thomas Fuller and popularized by Benjamin Franklin in 1737.

text: Better safe than sorry.
explanation: An early 19th-century English colloquial expression.

text: Misery loves company.
explanation: Traced to Publilius Syrus and Christopher Marlowe's Doctor Faustus (1592).

text: No pain, no gain.
explanation: Popularized by Benjamin Franklin in The Way to Wealth (1758).

text: Opposites attract.
explanation: A 19th-century scientific physics metaphor applied to romance.

text: Out of sight, out of mind.
explanation: Recorded in John Heywood's 1546 collection and Homer's Odyssey.

text: The early bird catches the worm.
explanation: Recorded in William Camden's 1605 Remaines of a Greater Worke.

text: You can lead a horse to water, but you can't make him drink.
explanation: Recorded in Old English in John Heywood's 1546 collection.

text: All's fair in love and war.
explanation: Coined by John Lyly in Euphues: The Anatomy of Wit (1579).

text: Barking up the wrong tree.
explanation: An early 19th-century American hunting idiom.

text: Bite off more than you can chew.
explanation: A late 19th-century American tobacco-chewing idiom.

text: Burn the candle at both ends.
explanation: From Edna St. Vincent Millay's 1920 poem First Fig.

text: Cry over spilled milk.
explanation: Recorded in James Howell's 1659 proverb collection.

text: Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
explanation: From Miguel de Cervantes' Don Quixote (1605).

text: Fit as a fiddle.
explanation: Recorded in William Haughton's 1600 play Englishmen for My Money.

text: Hit the nail on the head.
explanation: Recorded in Margery Kempe's 1438 book.

text: In the heat of the moment.
explanation: A 19th-century legal and literary English phrase.

text: Keep your chin up.
explanation: An early 20th-century English encouragement idiom.

text: Let sleeping dogs lie.
explanation: Found in Geoffrey Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1385).

text: Once in a blue moon.
explanation: Recorded in an anti-clerical 1528 pamphlet by William Roy.

text: Piece of cake.
explanation: Originated in American 1930s cakewalk dances and Ogden Nash poetry.

text: A house divided against itself cannot stand.
explanation: Mark 3:25 and Matthew 12:25, spoken by Jesus when answering the scribes.
misconception: Many believe Abraham Lincoln wrote it in 1858; he was quoting Jesus.

text: The truth shall make you free.
explanation: John 8:32, Jesus speaking to those who believed in Him.
misconception: Often inscribed on secular university gates.

text: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son.
explanation: John 3:16, Jesus speaking to Nicodemus.
misconception: The most famous gospel verse in history.

text: I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.
explanation: Philippians 4:13, Paul writing from prison in Rome.

text: Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.
explanation: Proverbs 3:5, King Solomon's foundational wisdom advice.

text: A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
explanation: Proverbs 15:1, Solomon's teaching on gentle speech.

text: Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
explanation: Proverbs 27:17, celebrating godly brotherhood and counsel.

text: Where there is no vision, the people perish.
explanation: Proverbs 29:18, emphasizing spiritual guidance and prophetic revelation.

text: Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
explanation: Galatians 6:7, Paul instructing the churches of Galatia.
misconception: Often confused with Eastern karma concepts.

text: Be sure your sin will find you out.
explanation: Numbers 32:23, Moses addressing the tribes of Reuben and Gad.

text: The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.
explanation: Psalm 23:1, King David's famous psalm of trust.
misconception: Most memorized psalm in the Bible.

text: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?
explanation: Jeremiah 13:23, prophet Jeremiah on persistent disobedience.
misconception: Often assumed to be an Aesop fable.

text: Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing.
explanation: Matthew 7:15, Jesus teaching on discernment in the Sermon on the Mount.
misconception: Source of the idiom 'wolf in sheep's clothing'.

text: Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin: the writing on the wall.
explanation: Daniel 5:5 & 5:25, God's judgment during King Belshazzar's banquet.
misconception: Origin of 'the writing on the wall'.

text: I am escaped with the skin of my teeth.
explanation: Job 19:20, Job lamenting his physical afflictions and close brush with death.
misconception: Widely thought to be modern American slang.

text: Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket.
explanation: Isaiah 40:15, Isaiah magnifying God's majesty over empires.
misconception: Origin of 'a drop in the bucket'.

text: If the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch.
explanation: Matthew 15:14 and Luke 6:39, Jesus exposing the religious hypocrisy of the Pharisees.
misconception: Famous worldwide proverb coined by Jesus.

text: Ye are the salt of the earth.
explanation: Matthew 5:13, Jesus addressing His disciples on their preservative influence in the world.
misconception: Origin of the phrase 'salt of the earth'.

text: Eat, drink, and be merry.
explanation: Ecclesiastes 8:15 and Luke 12:19, describing earthly pleasure and vanity.
misconception: Found in both the Old and New Testaments.

text: Keep me as the apple of the eye.
explanation: Psalm 17:8 and Deuteronomy 32:10, describing God's pupil of vision and tender care.
misconception: Origin of the beloved English idiom.

text: Am I my brother's keeper?
explanation: Genesis 4:9, Cain's defiant question to God after slaying Abel.
misconception: Found in the first book of the Bible.

text: There is no new thing under the sun.
explanation: Ecclesiastes 1:9, Solomon's reflection on repetitive history.
misconception: Origin of 'nothing new under the sun'.

text: Whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.
explanation: Matthew 5:39, Jesus teaching kingdom meekness and non-retaliation.

text: He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.
explanation: John 8:7, Jesus confronting the accusers of the adulterous woman.

text: Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.
explanation: Deuteronomy 8:3 and Matthew 4:4, Jesus quoting Moses to rebuke Satan.
misconception: Found in both Deuteronomy and the Gospels.

text: Neither cast ye your pearls before swine.
explanation: Matthew 7:6, Jesus warning against giving holy things to those who despise them.

text: For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life.
explanation: Romans 6:23, Paul's classic gospel contrast in Romans.

text: Faith without works is dead.
explanation: James 2:20 & 2:26, James demonstrating the inseparable fruit of genuine faith.
misconception: A prominent doctrine in the Epistle of James.

text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
explanation: John 1:1, the prologue of the Gospel of John testifying of Christ's eternal deity.

text: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
explanation: Genesis 1:1, the opening verse of the Christian and Jewish canon.
misconception: The very first sentence in the Bible.

text: Fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.
explanation: Psalm 111:10 and Proverbs 9:10, foundational Old Testament wisdom truth.
misconception: A recurring theme across Hebrew wisdom literature.

text: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
explanation: Matthew 11:28, Jesus's gracious invitation to weary souls.

text: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.
explanation: Matthew 7:7, Jesus teaching persistent prayer.
misconception: The ASK promise in the Sermon on the Mount.

text: I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
explanation: John 14:6, Jesus speaking to Thomas in the Upper Room.

text: We walk by faith, not by sight.
explanation: 2 Corinthians 5:7, Paul encouraging believers regarding their eternal home.

text: The Lord bless thee, and keep thee: The Lord make his face shine upon thee.
explanation: Numbers 6:24-25, the Aaronic priestly benediction.

text: He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters.
explanation: Psalm 23:2, David's pastoral psalm of divine peace.

text: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
explanation: Psalm 119:105, extolling the clarity and illumination of God's Word.
misconception: From the longest chapter in the Bible.

text: Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
explanation: Psalm 51:10, David's repentant prayer after his sin with Bathsheba.

text: Cast thy burden upon the Lord, and he shall sustain thee.
explanation: Psalm 55:22, David encouraging the believer in distress.

text: As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.
explanation: Psalm 42:1, sons of Korah describing spiritual thirst.

text: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
explanation: Psalm 46:1, inspiring Martin Luther's hymn 'A Mighty Fortress'.

text: O taste and see that the Lord is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him.
explanation: Psalm 34:8, David praising God when pretending madness before Abimelech.

text: Delight thyself also in the Lord; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart.
explanation: Psalm 37:4, David teaching patient trust in God's timing.

text: I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.
explanation: Psalm 139:14, David meditating on God's omniscient creation of life.

text: The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
explanation: Psalm 19:1, David praising God's universal revelation in nature.

text: As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
explanation: Joshua 24:15, Joshua's farewell covenant challenge at Shechem.

text: Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed.
explanation: Joshua 1:9, God commissioning Joshua after the death of Moses.
misconception: Command to Joshua leading Israel into Canaan.

text: The name of the Lord is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
explanation: Proverbs 18:10, Solomon teaching the refuge of God's character.

text: Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
explanation: Proverbs 22:6, biblical parenting maxim.

text: Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.
explanation: Proverbs 6:6, Solomon rebuking laziness through nature observation.

text: He that watereth shall be watered also himself.
explanation: Proverbs 11:25, Solomon on the blessing of generous living.

text: Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
explanation: Proverbs 16:18, exact King James phrasing of the famous proverb.
misconception: The authentic biblical source of the common idiom.

text: A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
explanation: Proverbs 17:17, celebrating covenant friendship.

text: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine.
explanation: Proverbs 17:22, Solomon observing the health benefits of joyful spirit.

text: He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the Lord.
explanation: Proverbs 19:17, divine reward for helping those in need.
misconception: Proverb on caring for the needy.

text: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.
explanation: Ecclesiastes 3:1, Solomon's reflection on the divinely appointed seasons of life.

text: A threefold cord is not quickly broken.
explanation: Ecclesiastes 4:12, praising unity and cooperative companionship.
misconception: Frequently used in Christian wedding ceremonies.

text: Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days.
explanation: Ecclesiastes 11:1, encouraging generous, faith-filled venture.

text: Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth.
explanation: Ecclesiastes 12:1, urging early devotion before aging sets in.

text: They that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles.
explanation: Isaiah 40:31, prophet Isaiah comforting weary exiles.

text: Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God.
explanation: Isaiah 41:10, God promising personal presence and help.

text: He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities.
explanation: Isaiah 53:5, prophetic depiction of the suffering Servant of God.

text: Seek ye the Lord while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near.
explanation: Isaiah 55:6, urgent call to repentance and divine fellowship.

text: For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the Lord, thoughts of peace, and not of evil.
explanation: Jeremiah 29:11, God's promise to Babylonian exiles.
misconception: One of the most frequently quoted verses in Scripture.

text: Call unto me, and I will answer thee, and shew thee great and mighty things.
explanation: Jeremiah 33:3, God speaking to Jeremiah in the court of the prison.

text: It is of the Lord's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.
explanation: Lamentations 3:22, Jeremiah's hope amidst the ashes of Jerusalem.
misconception: Origin of the hymn 'Great is Thy Faithfulness'.

text: They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
explanation: Lamentations 3:23, declaration of God's daily fresh mercies.
misconception: Found in the Book of Lamentations.

text: He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
explanation: Micah 6:8, prophet Micah summarizing true spiritual worship.

text: The just shall live by his faith.
explanation: Habakkuk 2:4, quoted by Paul in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11.
misconception: Foundational verse of the Protestant Reformation.

text: Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts.
explanation: Zechariah 4:6, God's word to Zerubbabel regarding rebuilding the temple.

text: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
explanation: Matthew 5:3, the first Beatitude in the Sermon on the Mount.

text: Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
explanation: Matthew 5:9, Beatitude praising those who actively make peace.

text: Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works.
explanation: Matthew 5:16, Jesus commanding transparent holy living.
misconception: Follows 'ye are the light of the world'.

text: Seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.
explanation: Matthew 6:33, Jesus teaching freedom from anxiety over material needs.

text: Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself.
explanation: Matthew 6:34, Jesus commanding believers not to worry about tomorrow.
misconception: Conclusion of Jesus's discourse on anxiety.

text: Judge not, that ye be not judged.
explanation: Matthew 7:1, opening command of Matthew chapter 7.
misconception: Frequently quoted and debated verse on judgment.

text: The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few.
explanation: Matthew 9:37, Jesus looking with compassion on the multitudes.

text: With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.
explanation: Matthew 19:26, Jesus answering His disciples regarding salvation.

text: Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.
explanation: Matthew 24:35, Jesus declaring the eternal endurance of His teachings.
misconception: Solemn guarantee of Christ's eternal Word.

text: God works in mysterious ways, his wonders to perform.
explanation: Written by English poet William Cowper in his 1773 hymn 'Light Shining Out of Darkness'.
misconception: Vastly believed to be a direct biblical quote.

text: The devil made me do it.
explanation: Popularized by comedian Flip Wilson on television in the 1970s; Genesis 3:13 has Eve saying 'the serpent beguiled me'.

text: To the pure, all things are pure, and to the dirty, all things are dirty.
explanation: Titus 1:15 says 'Unto the pure all things are pure: but unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure.'

text: God never closes a door without opening a window.
explanation: Folk optimism adage dating from late 19th-century America.

text: Money makes the world go round.
explanation: From John Kander and Fred Ebb's 1966 musical Cabaret.

text: Praise the Lord and pass the ammunition.
explanation: A 1942 American patriotic song by Frank Loesser written after Pearl Harbor.

text: The way to a man's heart is through his stomach.
explanation: First recorded in 1814 by English novelist Sarah Stickney Ellis.

text: Spare no expense.
explanation: An English idiom popularized in modern cinema (Jurassic Park) and late 19th-century fiction.

text: Children should be seen and not heard.
explanation: A 15th-century English proverb originally written 'Hlystre hit mehte, seon he ne mihte'.

text: The road to hell is paved with good intentions.
explanation: Attributed to Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (c. 1150) and Samuel Johnson (1775).

text: Moderation in all things.
explanation: A classical Greek maxim attributed to Hesiod, Cleobulus, and Roman poet Terence.

text: An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.
explanation: Coined by Benjamin Franklin in 1736 concerning fire safety in Philadelphia.

text: Beauty is only skin deep.
explanation: Written by English poet Sir Thomas Overbury in 1613.

text: Cross my heart and hope to die.
explanation: A 19th-century schoolyard oath originating in Catholic gestures.

text: You can't take it with you.
explanation: Popularized by George S. Kaufman and Moss Hart's 1936 play. 1 Timothy 6:7 says 'we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.'

text: Like a moth to a flame.
explanation: Traced to Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice (Act 2, Scene 9).

text: Misfortunes never come singly.
explanation: First recorded in 1612 in Thomas Shelton's translation of Don Quixote.

text: Every man has his price.
explanation: Attributed to British Prime Minister Sir Robert Walpole in 1734.

text: Fools rush in where angels fear to tread.
explanation: Written by Alexander Pope in his 1711 poem An Essay on Criticism.

text: Great minds think alike.
explanation: Recorded in English in 1816 in Dabney Carr's letters.

text: Hope for the best, prepare for the worst.
explanation: Coined by English novelist Benjamin Disraeli in The Wondrous Tale of Alroy (1833).

text: Necessity is the mother of invention.
explanation: Traced to Plato's Republic and Richard Franck's Northern Memoirs (1658).

text: No news is good news.
explanation: First recorded in English in 1616 in letters of King James I.

text: Patience solves all problems.
explanation: A Latin motto from Cato's Distichs.

text: Power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.
explanation: Written by Lord Acton in an 1887 letter to Bishop Mandell Creighton.

text: The customer is always right.
explanation: Coined by department store pioneer Harry Gordon Selfridge in 1909.

text: The end justifies the means.
explanation: Commonly attributed to Niccolò Machiavelli in The Prince (1532) and Roman poet Ovid.

text: The greatest thing you'll ever learn is just to love and be loved in return.
explanation: Written by Eden Ahbez in the 1947 song Nature Boy.

text: There but for the grace of God go I.
explanation: Attributed to English Protestant reformer John Bradford (c. 1550) upon seeing criminals led to execution.

text: Time is money.
explanation: Coined by Benjamin Franklin in Advice to a Young Tradesman (1748).

text: Too good to be true.
explanation: First recorded in 1580 by English writer Thomas Lupton.

text: Variety is the spice of life.
explanation: Written by William Cowper in his 1785 poem The Task.

text: Wear your heart on your sleeve.
explanation: Written by William Shakespeare in Othello (Act 1, Scene 1).

text: You reap what you don't sow.
explanation: A distortion of Galatians 6:7. The Bible actually says 'whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.'

text: A picture is worth a thousand words.
explanation: Coined by advertising executive Fred R. Barnard in Printers' Ink (1921).

text: All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy.
explanation: First recorded in James Howell's Proverbs (1659).

text: An apple a day keeps the doctor away.
explanation: Originated in Wales in the 1860s as 'Eat an apple on going to bed'.

text: As comfortable as an old shoe.
explanation: An early 20th-century American colloquial comparison.

text: As pure as the driven snow.
explanation: Found in Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale (Act 4, Scene 4). Isaiah 1:18 says 'they shall be as white as snow.'

text: At the drop of a hat.
explanation: An American 19th-century signal idiom for beginning a race or fight.

text: Back to square one.
explanation: Originated in BBC radio commentary grids for football matches in the 1930s.

text: Bark is worse than his bite.
explanation: Recorded in George Herbert's Outlandish Proverbs (1640).

text: Beat around the bush.
explanation: From George Gascoigne's 1572 poem on bird hunting.

text: Behind every great man there is a great woman.
explanation: First recorded in mid-20th century American newspapers.

text: Best of both worlds.
explanation: From late 19th-century English literary criticism.

text: Bite the bullet.
explanation: Derived from military battlefield surgeries before modern anesthesia.

text: Break the ice.
explanation: Written by William Shakespeare in The Taming of the Shrew (Act 1, Scene 2).

text: Burn bridges behind you.
explanation: Derived from ancient military tactics of burning bridges to prevent retreat.

text: Bury the hatchet.
explanation: A Native American ceremony among the Iroquois peace confederacy.

text: By hook or by crook.
explanation: Medieval English forest law permitting peasants to collect wood reachable by a hook or shepherd's crook.

text: Call a spade a spade.
explanation: Traced to Plutarch's Apophthegmata and Erasmus's Adagia (1500).

text: Caught red-handed.
explanation: An ancient Scottish legal term for finding a slaughterer with the blood still on his hands.

text: Close, but no cigar.
explanation: Originated in American fairground carnival games where cigars were prizes.

text: Cold feet.
explanation: Recorded in Fritz Reuter's 1862 German novel and Stephen Crane's Maggie (1896).

text: Cost an arm and a leg.
explanation: Originated in post-World War II American slang referring to casualty costs.

text: Devil's advocate.
explanation: The official title (Advocatus Diaboli) established by Pope Sixtus V in 1587 to argue against canonization.

text: Down to the wire.
explanation: Late 19th-century American horse-racing slang referring to the finish line wire.

text: Drive someone up the wall.
explanation: Mid-20th century American slang.

text: Drop the ball.
explanation: Originated in American football and baseball commentary.

text: Elephant in the room.
explanation: First recorded in Mark Twain's writings and popularized in the 1950s.

text: Face the music.
explanation: An American theatrical and military marching idiom from the 1850s.

text: Fish out of water.
explanation: Recorded in Geoffrey Chaucer's Canterbury Tales (c. 1387).

text: Flash in the pan.
explanation: Refers to 17th-century flintlock muskets when priming powder flared without firing the ball.

text: Fly off the handle.
explanation: 19th-century American frontier slang referring to an axe-head flying loose.

text: Foot in the door.
explanation: An early 20th-century door-to-door salesman technique.

text: Get your ducks in a row.
explanation: Originated in American bowling games or tin-duck shooting galleries.

text: Grasp at straws.
explanation: From Thomas More's A Dialogue of Comfort Against Tribulation (1534).

text: Graveyard shift.
explanation: An early 20th-century American workplace idiom for the midnight-to-dawn shift.

text: Head over heels.
explanation: Originally 'heels over head' in 14th-century English, modern inversion in the 1800s.

text: Hear it through the grapevine.
explanation: American Civil War slang referring to makeshift telegraph wires looking like grapevines.

text: Hit the sack.
explanation: Early 20th-century American military slang referring to canvas bed sacks.

text: Hold your horses.
explanation: 19th-century American frontier coaching command.

text: In a nutshell.
explanation: Traced to Pliny the Elder and William Shakespeare's Hamlet.

text: In cahoots with someone.
explanation: Early 19th-century American frontier slang derived from French 'cahute' (cabin).

text: It takes two to tango.
explanation: From the 1952 American pop song by Al Hoffman and Dick Manning.

text: Jump on the bandwagon.
explanation: Originated with Dan Rice's 1848 political campaign wagon for Zachary Taylor.

text: Keep your fingers crossed.
explanation: Pre-Christian European and medieval gesture invoking good fortune.

text: Kick the bucket.
explanation: Late 18th-century English slang derived from slaughterhouse hanging beams.

text: Left in the lurch.
explanation: Originated in the 16th-century French board game Lourche.

text: Let the cat out of the bag.
explanation: From medieval market swindles where cats were substituted for suckling pigs in bags.

text: A thorn in the flesh.
explanation: 2 Corinthians 12:7, Paul describing his mysterious bodily affliction.
misconception: Origin of 'a thorn in my side/flesh'.

text: Gird up the loins of your mind.
explanation: 1 Peter 1:13 and Job 38:3, biblical command to prepare mental faculties for action.
misconception: Origin of the phrase 'gird your loins'.

text: In the twinkling of an eye.
explanation: 1 Corinthians 15:52, Paul describing the sudden transformation of believers at Christ's return.
misconception: Origin of 'in the twinkling of an eye'.

text: Fly in the ointment.
explanation: Ecclesiastes 10:1: 'Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour.'
misconception: Origin of 'a fly in the ointment'.

text: The powers that be.
explanation: Romans 13:1: 'The powers that be are ordained of God.'

text: At their wit's end.
explanation: Psalm 107:27, describing mariners caught in a violent sea tempest.

text: Put words in his mouth.
explanation: 2 Samuel 14:3, Joab commanding the wise woman of Tekoa regarding King David.
misconception: Origin of 'putting words in my mouth'.

text: Fall from grace.
explanation: Galatians 5:4: 'Ye are fallen from grace.'

text: Straight and narrow.
explanation: Matthew 7:14: 'Straight is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life.'
misconception: Origin of 'on the straight and narrow'.

text: See eye to eye.
explanation: Isaiah 52:8: 'Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice... for they shall see eye to eye.'

text: A man after his own heart.
explanation: 1 Samuel 13:14 and Acts 13:22, describing King David's devotion to God.
misconception: Origin of 'a man after my own heart'.

text: Nothing but skin and bones.
explanation: Job 19:20 and Psalm 102:5, poetically describing extreme wasting.

text: Out of the mouths of babes and sucklings hast thou ordained strength.
explanation: Psalm 8:2, quoted by Jesus in Matthew 21:16.
misconception: Origin of 'out of the mouths of babes'.

text: Peace on earth, good will toward men.
explanation: Luke 2:14, the heavenly host praising God at the birth of Jesus.

text: Physician, heal thyself.
explanation: Luke 4:23, quoted by Jesus in the synagogue at Nazareth.

text: Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
explanation: Matthew 26:52, Jesus rebuking Peter at Gethsemane.
misconception: Origin of 'live by the sword, die by the sword'.

text: The root of the matter.
explanation: Job 19:28: 'Seeing the root of the matter is found in me.'

text: Signs of the times.
explanation: Matthew 16:3: 'Can ye not discern the signs of the times?'
misconception: Jesus rebuking the Pharisees and Sadducees.

text: For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind.
explanation: Hosea 8:7, Hosea's prophecy against Israel's idolatry.

text: The staff of bread.
explanation: Ezekiel 4:16 and Leviticus 26:26: 'I will break the staff of bread.'

text: A stumbling stone and rock of offence.
explanation: Isaiah 8:14 and Romans 9:33, describing Christ as a rock of stumbling to unbelief.

text: The voice of one crying in the wilderness.
explanation: Isaiah 40:3 and Matthew 3:3, describing John the Baptist preparing the way of the Lord.

text: Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.
explanation: Isaiah 1:18, God inviting Israel to reason and receive cleansing.

text: Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips.
explanation: Isaiah 6:5, Isaiah's cry of conviction before the throne of God.

text: Here am I; send me.
explanation: Isaiah 6:8, Isaiah's willing response to God's heavenly commission.

text: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
explanation: Jeremiah 17:9, Jeremiah's profound diagnosis of fallen human nature.

text: Can two walk together, except they be agreed?
explanation: Amos 3:3, prophet Amos on spiritual agreement and covenant alignment.

text: Prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.
explanation: Amos 4:12, Amos's solemn prophetic summons to the northern kingdom.

text: Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me.
explanation: Malachi 3:8, Malachi confronting the priesthood regarding tithes and offerings.
misconception: Foundational verse on tithing in Malachi.

text: The Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings.
explanation: Malachi 4:2, messianic promise closing the Old Testament canon.
misconception: Closing messianic prophecy of the OT.

text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the Lord.
explanation: Malachi 4:5, final prophecy of the Old Testament.

text: Be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
explanation: Matthew 10:16, Jesus commissioning the Twelve disciples for mission.

text: Even the very hairs of your head are all numbered.
explanation: Matthew 10:30, Jesus teaching God's intimate providential care.

text: He that findeth his life shall lose it: and he that loseth his life for my sake shall find it.
explanation: Matthew 10:39, Jesus defining true discipleship.

text: A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench.
explanation: Isaiah 42:3 and Matthew 12:20, messianic tenderness toward the broken.
misconception: Prophetic portrayal of Christ's gentle mercy.

text: Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.
explanation: Matthew 12:34, Jesus demonstrating that words reveal inner spiritual character.
misconception: Profound psychological truth spoken by Christ.

text: Whosoever hath, to him shall be given, and he shall have more abundance.
explanation: Matthew 13:12, Jesus explaining the spiritual law of receptivity in parables.

text: Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church.
explanation: Matthew 16:18, Jesus's declaration at Caesarea Philippi.

text: What shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?
explanation: Mark 8:36 and Matthew 16:26, Jesus measuring the supreme value of the human soul.

text: If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence.
explanation: Matthew 17:20, Jesus teaching the dynamic power of living faith.

text: Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
explanation: Matthew 18:20, Jesus promising His presence in church fellowship.

text: How often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times? Jesus saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.
explanation: Matthew 18:21-22, Jesus teaching unlimited forgiveness.

text: What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.
explanation: Matthew 19:6 and Mark 10:9, Jesus establishing the sacred permanency of marriage.

text: The last shall be first, and the first last.
explanation: Matthew 20:16, Jesus concluding the parable of the workers in the vineyard.

text: Many are called, but few are chosen.
explanation: Matthew 22:14, concluding the parable of the wedding banquet.
misconception: Solemn conclusion of the royal wedding banquet parable.

text: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment.
explanation: Matthew 22:37-38, Jesus quoting the Shema (Deut 6:5).

text: And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
explanation: Matthew 22:39, Jesus quoting Leviticus 19:18.
misconception: The Royal Law of neighbor love.

text: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law.
explanation: Matthew 23:23, Jesus exposing superficial legalism.
misconception: The weightier matters of the law.

text: Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel.
explanation: Matthew 23:24, Jesus's vivid humorous imagery against legalism.

text: Whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased; and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted.
explanation: Matthew 23:12, universal kingdom principle of humility.
misconception: Kingdom law of exaltation and humility.

text: Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things.
explanation: Matthew 25:21, the master's commendation in the parable of the talents.
misconception: The ultimate commendation of the disciple.

text: Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
explanation: Matthew 25:40, the King addressing the sheep on the throne of glory.
misconception: Identifying Christ with the poor and afflicted.

text: The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.
explanation: Matthew 26:41, Jesus cautioning Peter, James, and John at Gethsemane.
misconception: Spoken during the agony in Gethsemane.

text: All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth. Go ye therefore, and teach all nations.
explanation: Matthew 28:18-19, opening of the Great Commission.
misconception: The Great Commission of the resurrected Christ.

text: Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world.
explanation: Matthew 28:20, closing promise of the Gospel of Matthew.
misconception: The parting promise of Jesus in Matthew.

text: The Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath.
explanation: Mark 2:27, Jesus liberating the Sabbath from oppressive rabbinic burdens.

text: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.
explanation: Mark 9:24, the desperate father of the possessed boy crying out to Jesus.

text: With God nothing shall be impossible.
explanation: Luke 1:37, the angel Gabriel answering Mary at the Annunciation.
misconception: Spoken by Gabriel to the Virgin Mary.

text: My soul doth magnify the Lord, and my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour.
explanation: Luke 1:46-47, the opening lines of the Magnificat.
misconception: Mary's hymn of praise in Luke 1.

text: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.
explanation: Luke 2:14, the Gloria in Excelsis Deo sung by the angels.

text: Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word.
explanation: Luke 2:29, the Nunc Dimittis prayed by righteous Simeon.

text: Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over.
explanation: Luke 6:38, Jesus teaching the boundless generosity of God.

text: Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.
explanation: Luke 10:20, Jesus instructing the Seventy when returning from mission.
misconception: Jesus's counsel on the true source of joy.

text: Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.
explanation: Luke 23:34, Jesus's first word from the cross at Calvary.

text: Today shalt thou be with me in paradise.
explanation: Luke 23:43, Jesus's promise to the repentant thief on the cross.

text: Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.
explanation: Luke 23:46, Jesus's final word before yielding up His spirit.
misconception: Jesus quoting Psalm 31:5 on the cross.

text: Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?
explanation: Luke 24:32, the two disciples on the road to Emmaus.

text: He must increase, but I must decrease.
explanation: John 3:30, John the Baptist testifying of his submission to Jesus.

text: God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
explanation: John 4:24, Jesus teaching the Samaritan woman at Jacob's well.

text: I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger.
explanation: John 6:35, Jesus's first 'I AM' declaration after feeding the five thousand.
misconception: First of the seven 'I AM' statements in John.

text: I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness.
explanation: John 8:12, Jesus speaking at the Feast of Tabernacles.

text: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
explanation: John 10:11, Jesus contrasting Himself with hirelings.

text: I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live.
explanation: John 11:25, Jesus consoling Martha before raising Lazarus.

text: Jesus wept.
explanation: John 11:35, the shortest verse in the English Bible, showing Christ's deep human compassion at Lazarus's tomb.
misconception: Shortest verse in the English Bible.

text: A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you.
explanation: John 13:34, Jesus giving the Mandatum at the Last Supper.
misconception: The Mandatum novum of the Upper Room.

text: In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you.
explanation: John 14:2, Jesus comforting His disciples about their heavenly dwelling.

text: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you.
explanation: John 14:27, Jesus imparting His supernatural peace.
misconception: Gift of divine peace in John 14.

text: I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit.
explanation: John 15:5, Jesus teaching spiritual abiding and fruitfulness.

text: Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
explanation: John 15:13, Jesus teaching the ultimate measure of sacrificial love.

text: It is finished.
explanation: John 19:30, Jesus's triumphant victory cry (Tetelestai) upon the cross.
misconception: The Greek tetelestai: paid in full.

text: The word 'Trinity'.
explanation: The doctrine of the Triune God (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) is thoroughly biblical (Matthew 28:19, 2 Cor 13:14), but the specific word 'Trinity' (Trinitas) was coined by theologian Tertullian around 210 AD.
misconception: Many assume the exact word 'Trinity' appears in the Epistles.

text: The word 'Rapture'.
explanation: Derived from the Latin Vulgate 'rapiemur' in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 (Greek: harpagēsometha, 'caught up'), but the English word 'rapture' never appears in King James or modern English Bibles.
misconception: The concept is biblical, but the word itself is Latinate.

text: The word 'Purgatory'.
explanation: A medieval Catholic doctrine formalized at the Council of Florence (1439) and Council of Trent; the word is never found in scripture.
misconception: Not found in the biblical text.

text: The word 'Bible'.
explanation: Derived from the Greek 'ta biblia' (the books), originating from the Phoenician port city of Byblos; the word itself never appears inside the biblical text.
misconception: The book does not name itself 'The Bible'.

text: Delilah personally cut Samson's hair.
explanation: Judges 16:19 says: 'She made him sleep upon her knees; and she called for a man, and she caused him to shave off the seven locks of his head.'
misconception: Delilah called a barber/servant to shave him.

text: Noah took animals into the ark only two by two.
explanation: Genesis 7:2-3 clarifies that Noah took seven pairs of every clean animal and birds, and only one pair of unclean animals.
misconception: Children's books simplify the story to two of each.

text: Money is the root of all happiness.
explanation: A cynical commercial inversion of 1 Timothy 6:10.

text: The forbidden fruit was a pomegranate.
explanation: Jewish midrashic tradition suggests figs, wheat, or pomegranates, but Genesis 3:6 says only 'the fruit of the tree'.

text: Mary Magdalene was a prostitute.
explanation: Pope Gregory I conflated Mary Magdalene with the unnamed sinful woman in Luke 7 in a famous 591 AD homily; the Bible only says seven demons were cast out of her (Luke 8:2).

text: The Ten Commandments were written on two identical rectangular slabs.
explanation: The traditional arched tablet shape was created by 11th-century English illuminated manuscript illustrators; scripture describes tablets written on both sides (Exodus 32:15).
misconception: Medieval art created the dual rounded arch shape.

text: Salvation by works.
explanation: Ephesians 2:8-9 explicitly refutes this: 'For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.'

text: God created Lucifer as an archangel with musical pipes in his body.
explanation: Ezekiel 28:13 KJV mentions 'timbrels and pipes', but refers contextually to the Prince/King of Tyre's royal jewel-encrusted ornamentation.
misconception: Folk angelology based on poetic imagery.

text: Cleanliness is a cardinal virtue.
explanation: The four classical cardinal virtues are Prudence, Temperance, Fortitude, and Justice (from Plato and Ambrose).
misconception: Conflation of Wesley's adage and classical virtues.

text: There are nine choirs of angels named explicitly in one biblical list.
explanation: The celestial hierarchy (Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones, Dominions, Virtues, Powers, Principalities, Archangels, Angels) was systematized by Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite in the 5th century.

text: Saint Peter guards the pearly gates of heaven with a key.
explanation: Based on Jesus giving Peter 'the keys of the kingdom of heaven' in Matthew 16:19; Revelation 21:12 says twelve angels stand at the twelve gates.

text: Adam and Eve had only two sons: Cain and Abel.
explanation: Genesis 4:25 mentions Seth, and Genesis 5:4 states Adam 'begat sons and daughters.'
misconception: Folk retelling ignores Seth and the other children.

text: The ark of the covenant had wings made of real eagle feathers.
explanation: Exodus 25:18-20 specifies the cherubim wings were beaten out of pure solid gold.
misconception: Scripture states the cherubim were pure hammered gold.

text: Saul's name was changed to Paul because he converted.
explanation: Saul (Hebrew name) and Paul (Roman name, Paullus) were dual names he possessed from birth as a Roman citizen of Tarsus (Acts 13:9).
misconception: God never renames Saul in Acts, unlike Abram or Jacob.

text: Jesus was born on December 25th in year zero.
explanation: Scripture gives no calendar date (shepherds were in fields, pointing to spring or autumn), and historically there is no year zero (1 BC is followed by 1 AD).
misconception: December 25 was established in Rome in 336 AD.

text: Moses had literal animal horns growing from his forehead.
explanation: Saint Jerome mistranslated the Hebrew 'qaran' (shone/beamed with rays of light) in Exodus 34:29 as 'cornuta' (horned), leading Michelangelo to sculpt Moses with horns.
misconception: Famous Latin Vulgate mistranslation by Jerome.

text: The apple of discord.
explanation: From Greek mythology: the golden apple thrown by Eris at the wedding of Peleus.

text: Achilles' heel.
explanation: From the Greek myth of Achilles being dipped in the River Styx by his mother Thetis.

text: Pandora's box.
explanation: From Hesiod's Works and Days in Greek mythology.

text: The Midas touch.
explanation: From the Greek myth of King Midas of Phrygia.

text: Swan song.
explanation: From the ancient Greek belief that swans sing beautifully just before dying (Aesop, Aristotle).

text: Crocodile tears.
explanation: From the ancient belief that crocodiles weep while devouring their prey, found in 14th-century travels of Sir John Mandeville.

text: Phoenix rising from the ashes.
explanation: From ancient Egyptian and Greek mythology of the mythical firebird.

text: Trojan horse.
explanation: From Virgil's Aeneid and the Greek saga of the siege of Troy.

text: Sour grapes.
explanation: From Aesop's fable of The Fox and the Grapes.

text: Cry wolf.
explanation: From Aesop's fable of The Boy Who Cried Wolf.

text: Goose that laid the golden egg.
explanation: From Aesop's fable of greed.

text: Dog in the manger.
explanation: From a Greek fable in Lucian's Timon (2nd century AD).

text: Cat got your tongue?
explanation: A 19th-century English nursery idiom.

text: Raining cats and dogs.
explanation: First recorded in Jonathan Swift's 1738 Complete Collection of Genteel Conversation.

text: Spill the beans.
explanation: Originated in American 20th-century slang, possibly from ancient Greek voting beans.

text: Barking dogs seldom bite.
explanation: Recorded in Latin by Quintus Curtius Rufus in the 1st century AD.

text: Beauty without virtue is a flower without perfume.
explanation: A French proverb recorded by Madame de Scudéry in the 17th century.

text: Better to be alone than in bad company.
explanation: Written by George Washington in his Rules of Civility (1744).

text: Borrowed garments never fit well.
explanation: A Gaelic and Scottish proverb.

text: Constant dropping wears away a stone.
explanation: From Roman poet Lucretius in De Rerum Natura and Ovid.

text: Dead men tell no tales.
explanation: First recorded in 1665 in Scottish proverbs and pirate folklore.

text: Discretion is the better part of valor.
explanation: Spoken by Falstaff in Shakespeare's Henry IV, Part 1 (Act 5, Scene 4).

text: Do not look a gift horse in the mouth.
explanation: Recorded by Saint Jerome in 400 AD as an ancient common proverb.

text: Empty vessels make the most sound.
explanation: Recorded by Plato in The Laws and Shakespeare in Henry V.

text: Familiarity breeds contempt.
explanation: Traced to Publilius Syrus and Geoffrey Chaucer in The Tale of Melibee.

text: Finders keepers, losers weepers.
explanation: A Roman legal principle (lex inventores) turned into a 19th-century children's rhyme.

text: First come, first served.
explanation: Recorded in Chaucer's The Wife of Bath's Tale (c. 1386).

text: Gilded cage.
explanation: From Arthur J. Lamb's 1900 song 'A Bird in a Gilded Cage'.

text: Hair of the dog that bit you.
explanation: An ancient Roman folk medical superstition recorded by Pliny the Elder.

text: He who hesitates is lost.
explanation: From Joseph Addison's 1713 play Cato.

text: Haste makes waste.
explanation: Recorded in John Heywood's 1546 dialogue of proverbs.

text: He who laughs last laughs best.
explanation: From a 16th-century French comedy by Antoine de Baïf.

text: History repeats itself.
explanation: Coined in English by historian Thomas Carlyle and Samuel Butler.

text: If at first you don't succeed, try, try again.
explanation: Coined by Scottish teacher Thomas H. Palmer in The Teacher's Manual (1840).

text: If the shoe fits, wear it.
explanation: Derived from the 17th-century idiom 'if the cap fits, wear it'.

text: In the kingdom of the blind, the one-eyed man is king.
explanation: Recorded in Desiderius Erasmus's Adagia (1500).

text: It is easier said than done.
explanation: Traced to ancient Roman playwright Plautus.

text: Jack of all trades, master of none.
explanation: Recorded in English in 1612 by Geffray Mynshul.

text: Leopard cannot change his spots overnight.
explanation: Jeremiah 13:23 asks 'Can the leopard change his spots?'; the 'overnight' suffix is modern.

text: Let bygones be bygones.
explanation: Recorded in Robert Sanderson's Sermons in 1636.

text: Life is what happens while you are busy making other plans.
explanation: Written by Allen Saunders in Reader's Digest (1957) and popularized by John Lennon (1980).

text: Like father, like son.
explanation: Recorded in English in 1573 in Tusser's Five Hundred Points.

text: Live and let live.
explanation: Recorded in Gerard de Malynes's 1622 merchant treatise.

text: Make hay while the sun shines.
explanation: Recorded in John Heywood's 1546 proverb collection.

text: Man proposes, God disposes.
explanation: Written by Thomas à Kempis in The Imitation of Christ (1418, Book 1, Ch. 19). Proverbs 16:9 states the biblical concept.
misconception: Thomas à Kempis's Latin devotional phrasing.

text: Many hands make light work.
explanation: Recorded in John Heywood's 1546 collection.

text: Match made in heaven.
explanation: First recorded in 16th-century English romances.

text: Mind your P's and Q's.
explanation: 18th-century English pub slate accounting for pints and quarts.

text: More than one way to skin a cat.
explanation: Recorded in Charles Kingsley's 1855 novel Westward Ho!.

text: Never bite the hand that feeds you.
explanation: Recorded by Edmund Burke in Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents (1770).

text: Never judge a book by its cover.
explanation: First recorded in George Eliot's 1860 novel The Mill on the Floss and 1944 murder mystery.

text: No man is an island.
explanation: Written by English poet John Donne in Devotions upon Emergent Occasions (1624).

text: Off with his head!
explanation: From William Shakespeare's Richard III and Lewis Carroll's Alice in Wonderland.

text: Old habits die hard.
explanation: Recorded in 18th-century English correspondence.

text: One man's meat is another man's poison.
explanation: From Roman philosophical poet Lucretius in De Rerum Natura.

text: One swallow does not make a summer.
explanation: Attributed to Aristotle in Nicomachean Ethics (Book 1).

text: Open a can of worms.
explanation: Mid-20th century American fishing bait idiom.

text: Pave the way.
explanation: Traced to the 16th-century translation of Erasmus's works.

text: Pay the piper.
explanation: From the German legend of the Pied Piper of Hamelin (1284).

text: Penny wise, pound foolish.
explanation: Coined by Robert Burton in The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621).

text: The Lord shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace.
explanation: Exodus 14:14, Moses reassuring the trembling Israelites at the Red Sea.

text: The secret things belong unto the Lord our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us.
explanation: Deuteronomy 29:29, Moses defining the boundary of divine revelation.

text: Choose you this day whom ye will serve.
explanation: Joshua 24:15, Joshua challenging the twelve tribes at Shechem.

text: The Lord seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.
explanation: 1 Samuel 16:7, God correcting Samuel when selecting David over Eliab.

text: How long halt ye between two opinions? if the Lord be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him.
explanation: 1 Kings 18:21, Elijah challenging the nation of Israel on Mount Carmel.

text: And after the earthquake a fire; but the Lord was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.
explanation: 1 Kings 19:12, God revealing Himself to Elijah at Mount Horeb.

text: Let not him that girdeth on his harness boast himself as he that putteth it off.
explanation: 1 Kings 20:11, King Ahab's sharp warning to boastful Ben-hadad of Syria.

text: There be more with us than with him: with him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the Lord our God.
explanation: 2 Chronicles 32:7-8, King Hezekiah comforting Jerusalem against Sennacherib.

text: If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven.
explanation: 2 Chronicles 7:14, God's covenant response to Solomon's temple dedication.

text: The joy of the Lord is your strength.
explanation: Nehemiah 8:10, Nehemiah and Ezra comforting the weeping people after the Law was read.

text: Who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?
explanation: Esther 4:14, Mordecai challenging Queen Esther to plead for her people.
misconception: Famous quote from the Book of Esther.

text: The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.
explanation: Job 1:21, Job's worshipful response after losing his children and wealth.

text: Shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?
explanation: Job 2:10, Job correcting his wife's counsel to curse God.

text: Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.
explanation: Job 13:15, Job's resolute confession of trust amidst catastrophic agony.

text: I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth.
explanation: Job 19:25, Job's resurrection hope, inspiring Handel's Messiah.

text: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners.
explanation: Psalm 1:1, opening beatitude of the entire Book of Psalms.

text: Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way.
explanation: Psalm 2:12, messianic coronation psalm warning the rulers of the earth.

text: What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?
explanation: Psalm 8:4, David marveling at human significance in the vast cosmos.

text: The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God.
explanation: Psalm 14:1 and Psalm 53:1, David diagnosing practical and philosophical atheism.

text: The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage.
explanation: Psalm 16:6, David rejoicing in God's covenant allotment.

text: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
explanation: Psalm 22:1 and Matthew 27:46, prophetic cry of David quoted by Jesus on the cross.

text: The earth is the Lord's, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein.
explanation: Psalm 24:1, royal psalm of God's universal ownership of creation.

text: Who shall ascend into the hill of the Lord? or who shall stand in his holy place? He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart.
explanation: Psalm 24:3-4, entrance liturgy for worshippers of Yahweh.

text: The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?
explanation: Psalm 27:1, David's triumphant declaration of fearless trust.

text: One thing have I desired of the Lord, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the Lord.
explanation: Psalm 27:4, David's singular spiritual focus and longing.

text: Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
explanation: Psalm 30:5, David's testimony of God's restoration after chastening.

text: Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered.
explanation: Psalm 32:1, David's beatitude of justification, quoted in Romans 4:7.

text: I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread.
explanation: Psalm 37:25, David's lifelong observation of God's faithfulness.

text: Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen.
explanation: Psalm 46:10, God commanding raging nations to cease their warfare.
misconception: Command to rest in divine sovereignty.

text: The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.
explanation: Psalm 51:17, David recognizing the heart posture God truly desires.

text: He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
explanation: Psalm 91:1, opening line of the great psalm of divine refuge.

text: He shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.
explanation: Psalm 91:11, quoted by Satan in Matthew 4:6 when tempting Jesus.
misconception: Quoted by Satan in the wilderness.

text: Make a joyful noise unto the Lord, all ye lands. Serve the Lord with gladness.
explanation: Psalm 100:1-2, the jubilant psalm of thanksgiving.

text: Bless the Lord, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name.
explanation: Psalm 103:1, David summoning his entire being to praise God.

text: As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.
explanation: Psalm 103:12, infinite distance of God's complete forgiveness.

text: Like as a father pitieth his children, so the Lord pitieth them that fear him.
explanation: Psalm 103:13, God's paternal tender compassion.
misconception: Fatherhood of God in the Psalms.

text: The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.
explanation: Psalm 118:22, major messianic cornerstone prophecy quoted in the Gospels.

text: This is the day which the Lord hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.
explanation: Psalm 118:24, psalm of triumphant joy.

text: Except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it.
explanation: Psalm 127:1, Solomon's psalm of domestic and civic dependence on God.

text: Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.
explanation: Psalm 127:3, biblical view of the blessing of children.

text: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
explanation: Psalm 133:1, David's song of ascents celebrating holy covenant unity.

text: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion.
explanation: Psalm 137:1, the poignant lament of Hebrew exiles in Babylon.

text: How shall we sing the Lord's song in a strange land?
explanation: Psalm 137:4, exiles lamenting the loss of their sanctuary in Babylon.

text: If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; Even there shall thy hand lead me.
explanation: Psalm 139:9-10, David meditating on God's inescapable omnipresence.

text: Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts.
explanation: Psalm 139:23, David's voluntary surrender to divine examination.

text: Let everything that hath breath praise the Lord.
explanation: Psalm 150:6, the grand final doxology of the entire Psalter.
misconception: The very last verse of the Book of Psalms.

text: Buy the truth, and sell it not; also wisdom, and instruction, and understanding.
explanation: Proverbs 23:23, Solomon's counsel on the supreme value of spiritual truth.

text: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
explanation: Proverbs 25:11, Solomon describing timely, graceful speech.

text: If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink.
explanation: Proverbs 25:21, quoted by Paul in Romans 12:20.
misconception: Old Testament command to love enemies.

text: For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the Lord shall reward thee.
explanation: Proverbs 25:22 and Romans 12:20, convicting kindness overcoming malice.
misconception: Source of the 'coals of fire' idiom.

text: As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly.
explanation: Proverbs 26:11, quoted in 2 Peter 2:22 regarding apostates.

text: Boast not thyself of tomorrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth.
explanation: Proverbs 27:1, warning against arrogant presumption.

text: Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
explanation: Proverbs 27:6, true constructive friendship versus hypocritical flattery.

text: The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
explanation: Proverbs 28:1, psychological contrast between guilt and righteous courage.

text: He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
explanation: Proverbs 28:13, classic Old Testament doctrine of confession and mercy.

text: Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies.
explanation: Proverbs 31:10, opening of the famous acrostic ode to the noble wife.

text: Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised.
explanation: Proverbs 31:30, the spiritual climax of Proverbs 31.
misconception: Climax of the Book of Proverbs.

text: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.
explanation: Ecclesiastes 1:2 and 12:8, the recurring refrain of the Book of Ecclesiastes.

text: The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong.
explanation: Ecclesiastes 9:11, Solomon observing unpredictable human limitations.

text: Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days.
explanation: Ecclesiastes 11:1, encouraging generous, faith-filled venture.

text: Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.
explanation: Ecclesiastes 12:13, the ultimate theological verdict of Solomon.

text: For love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave.
explanation: Song of Solomon 8:6, poetry on the invincible power of covenant love.

text: Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.
explanation: Song of Solomon 8:7, poetic celebration of unyielding love.
misconception: Famous verse from Song of Solomon.

text: Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.
explanation: Isaiah 6:3 and Revelation 4:8, the angelic Trisagion before the throne.

text: Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
explanation: Isaiah 7:14, prophetic virgin birth sign given to King Ahaz.

text: For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder.
explanation: Isaiah 9:6, famous messianic prophecy of Christ's royal names.

text: And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
explanation: Isaiah 9:6, continuation of the royal messianic titles.

text: Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.
explanation: Isaiah 26:3, prophet Isaiah's promise of divine tranquility.

text: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
explanation: Isaiah 40:8, quoted in 1 Peter 1:24-25.

text: Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands; thy walls are continually before me.
explanation: Isaiah 49:16, God's affectionate response to Zion's cry of abandonment.
misconception: Prefiguring the nail marks of Christ.

text: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace.
explanation: Isaiah 52:7 and Romans 10:15, praising gospel messengers.

text: All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.
explanation: Isaiah 53:6, substitutionary atonement core text.

text: For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the Lord.
explanation: Isaiah 55:8, God's transcendence over finite human reasoning.

text: Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the Lord is risen upon thee.
explanation: Isaiah 60:1, prophetic summons to Zion in the messianic era.

text: The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek.
explanation: Isaiah 61:1, read by Jesus in the Nazareth synagogue (Luke 4:18).

text: Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee.
explanation: Jeremiah 1:5, God calling and ordaining the prophet Jeremiah.

text: My people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
explanation: Jeremiah 2:13, prophet Jeremiah diagnosing idolatrous futility.

text: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches: But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me.
explanation: Jeremiah 9:23-24, quoted in 1 Corinthians 1:31.

text: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel.
explanation: Jeremiah 31:31, first explicit Old Testament announcement of the New Covenant.
misconception: Old Testament prophecy of the New Covenant.

text: I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.
explanation: Jeremiah 31:33 and Hebrews 8:10, internal nature of the New Covenant.
misconception: Heart transformation under the New Covenant.

text: The word 'Lucifer' as the original personal name of Satan before the fall.
explanation: The word 'Lucifer' (Latin for 'light-bearer') appears only once in the King James Bible in Isaiah 14:12 translating the Hebrew 'Helel ben Shahar' (morning star, son of the dawn) addressed historically to the King of Babylon.
misconception: Scholars emphasize Isaiah 14 is a taunt against the King of Babylon.

text: The word 'Antichrist' appears in the Book of Revelation.
explanation: The specific word 'Antichrist' appears five times in the New Testament, but ONLY in the Epistles of 1 John and 2 John (e.g. 1 John 2:18, 4:3), NEVER in Revelation, which speaks of 'the Beast'.
misconception: Almost universally assumed to be a title in Revelation.

text: The word 'Omnipresent'.
explanation: While God's omnipresence is clearly taught (Psalm 139:7-10, Jeremiah 23:24), the Latinate systematic theology term 'omnipresent' never appears in scripture.

text: The word 'Omniscient'.
explanation: God's all-knowing nature is biblical truth (1 John 3:20, Hebrews 4:13), but the theological word 'omniscient' never occurs in the Bible.

text: The word 'Omnipotent'.
explanation: Appears only once in the KJV in Revelation 19:6 ('the Lord God omnipotent reigneth'); modern translations universally render it 'Almighty'.
misconception: Often thought to be ubiquitous in scripture.

text: There were three crosses on Mount Sinai.
explanation: The three crosses were on Golgotha/Calvary outside Jerusalem (John 19:17-18); Mount Sinai is where Moses received the Law in Exodus 19.

text: Potiphar's wife is named Zuleika in the Bible.
explanation: Genesis 39 never names Potiphar's wife; the name 'Zuleika' comes from Islamic tradition and Persian poetry (Yusuf and Zulaikha).
misconception: Named in Persian and Islamic lore, not in Genesis.

text: The forbidden fruit gave Adam and Eve special magical powers.
explanation: Genesis 3:7 says their eyes were opened to their own nakedness and guilt, not magical powers.

text: Goliath was slain by David's sword initially.
explanation: 1 Samuel 17:50 explicitly states: 'So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone... but there was no sword in the hand of David.' He later used Goliath's own sword to decapitate him.

text: The walls of Jericho fell down from the loud volume of the trumpets alone.
explanation: Joshua 6:20 states the people shouted with a great shout after the priests blew, and God caused the wall to fall down flat.

text: Methuselah was the oldest person who ever lived and died after the flood.
explanation: Methuselah died in the very year of the Great Flood before it began (Genesis 5:27, at age 969).
misconception: Died in the year of the flood.

text: Moses entered the Promised Land before he died.
explanation: Deuteronomy 34:4-5 states Moses viewed Canaan from Mount Nebo, but God did not permit him to cross over, and he died in Moab.
misconception: Moses died on Mount Nebo outside Canaan.

text: Elijah died in a fiery chariot accident.
explanation: 2 Kings 2:11 says Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven, while a chariot of fire separated him from Elisha.
misconception: He was taken up by a whirlwind into heaven without dying.

text: Enoch died of old age after walking with God.
explanation: Genesis 5:24 says: 'And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him.' Hebrews 11:5 confirms he did not see death.

text: Paul was struck blind by lightning on the Damascus road.
explanation: Acts 9:3 says: 'Suddenly there shined round about him a light from heaven.' No lightning or horse is mentioned in the text.
misconception: Artwork always depicts lightning and falling off a horse.

text: Paul was knocked off his horse on the road to Damascus.
explanation: Acts 9:4 and Acts 22:7 say he fell to the ground, but horses are never mentioned in any of the three conversion accounts.

text: There were two of every animal on the ark because God only made male and female.
explanation: Clean animals were taken by sevens (Genesis 7:2) to provide animals for sacrifice after the flood.
misconception: Clean animals were taken in sevens.

text: The fruit of the Spirit has nine separate fruits.
explanation: Galatians 5:22 uses the singular Greek word 'karpos' (fruit), not plural 'fruits', denoting a unified cluster.
misconception: Singular fruit, not nine separate fruits.

text: Jesus was an only child.
explanation: Mark 6:3 and Matthew 13:55-56 name his brothers James, Joses, Simon, and Judas, and mention his sisters.

text: Satan is pictured as having two goat horns, cloven hooves, and a tail.
explanation: Derived from Greek pagan god Pan and medieval mystery plays, not scripture.
