misconception: Pagan Pan iconography absorbed in medieval Europe.

text: A guardian angel is assigned to each person at birth with a personal clipboard.
explanation: Matthew 18:10 mentions angels who behold God's face, but personal assignment with clipboards is modern folklore.

text: The tree of life had golden leaves that healed mortal wounds instantly.
explanation: Revelation 22:2 says: 'The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations', without mentioning golden leaves or fantasy tropes.

text: Solomon wrote the entire Book of Psalms.
explanation: David wrote roughly half of them; others were written by Asaph, the sons of Korah, Moses (Psalm 90), Heman, Ethan, and Solomon (Psalms 72 & 127).
misconception: Multiple authors contributed to the Psalter.

text: The Bible is divided into 66 books in all traditions.
explanation: The Protestant canon has 66 books, but Catholic Bibles have 73 (including Deuterocanonical books), and Eastern Orthodox Bibles have up to 78 or more.
misconception: Canon counts vary across church traditions.

text: The original manuscripts of the Bible had chapter and verse numbers.
explanation: Stephen Langton (Archbishop of Canterbury) added chapter divisions in 1205, and French printer Robert Estienne added verses in 1551.
misconception: Chapters and verses were added in the 13th and 16th centuries.

text: All the apostles were martyred by violent execution.
explanation: Early church history universally records that the Apostle John died of natural old age in Ephesus or Patmos.
misconception: Apostle John died of natural old age.

text: Peter was crucified right side up in Rome.
explanation: Church tradition (Eusebius, Origen) records Peter requested to be crucified upside down, feeling unworthy to die like Christ.
misconception: Tradition records Peter was crucified upside down.

text: The Apostle Paul personally met Jesus during his earthly ministry.
explanation: Paul first encountered the resurrected Jesus on the Damascus road after the ascension (1 Corinthians 15:8).
misconception: Paul never met Jesus during His earthly pre-crucifixion life.

text: Nicodemus rejected Jesus and walked away into the dark.
explanation: John 19:39 shows Nicodemus boldly bringing 100 pounds of myrrh and aloes to assist Joseph of Arimathea in burying Jesus.
misconception: Nicodemus publicly assisted in Christ's burial.

text: The Ark of the Covenant was placed inside Solomon's second temple.
explanation: The Ark disappeared during the Babylonian destruction in 586 BC and was absent from the Second Temple (Herod's Temple).
misconception: The Holy of Holies in the Second Temple was empty.

text: The word 'Millennium'.
explanation: Revelation 20:2-7 speaks of 'a thousand years' six times, but the Latin derivative 'millennium' (mille + annus) is not an English Bible word.

text: The word 'Incarnation'.
explanation: John 1:14 teaches 'the Word became flesh', but the Latin systematic term 'incarnatio' does not appear in the text.

text: The word 'Monotheism'.
explanation: The concept is fundamental (Deuteronomy 6:4), but the Greek-derived word 'monotheism' was coined by English philosopher Henry More in 1660.

text: The word 'Eschatology'.
explanation: Coined in 1804 by German theologian Karl Philipp von Henke to denote the doctrine of last things.

text: The word 'Theodicy'.
explanation: Coined by German philosopher Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in 1710 in his work on God's justice.

text: The word 'Omnibenevolent'.
explanation: Modern philosophical term used to describe all-loving deity, coined in the 19th century.

text: The word 'Inerrancy'.
explanation: Formulated in modern scholastic Protestant theology during the Princeton debates of the 19th and 20th centuries.

text: The word 'Sola Scriptura'.
explanation: Latin slogan of the 16th-century Protestant Reformation, not a scriptural phrase.

text: The word 'Sola Fide'.
explanation: Latin Reformation phrase ('by faith alone'), formulated in the 1500s.

text: The word 'Sola Gratia'.
explanation: Latin Reformation phrase ('by grace alone').

text: The word 'Solus Christus'.
explanation: Latin Reformation phrase ('Christ alone').

text: The word 'Soli Deo Gloria'.
explanation: Latin Reformation phrase ('glory to God alone').

text: God tempers the wind to the shorn lamb.
explanation: Written by Laurence Sterne in A Sentimental Journey (1768), echoing a French proverb.

text: Cleanliness is next to sanctity.
explanation: Variation of Wesley's 1778 adage.

text: The road to paradise is paved with thorns.
explanation: A medieval monastic proverb.

text: God helps the sailor, but he must row.
explanation: A traditional Swedish and Breton fisherman's proverb.

text: Prayer changes things.
explanation: Popularized in 19th-century American revivalist mottoes and wall plaques.

text: Let go and let God.
explanation: Originated in the Higher Life / Keswick Movement in England in the 1870s.

text: Bloom where you are planted.
explanation: Attributed to Saint Francis de Sales (c. 1600) and popularized in 1970s Christian publishing.

text: God never closes a door without opening another door.
explanation: Folk optimism variant.

text: Heaven is a place where there are no clocks.
explanation: Folk sermon illustration, not biblical text.

text: Angels get their wings whenever a bell rings.
explanation: From Frank Capra's 1946 film It's a Wonderful Life.

text: Saint Michael holds the scales of judgment.
explanation: A medieval artistic depiction (psychostasis) derived from ancient Egyptian judgment scenes of Anubis.
misconception: Egyptian and medieval weighing of souls art.

text: The devil has two horns and a trident.
explanation: Absorbed from Neptune's trident and Pan's satyr appearance.

text: Judas hanged himself from an elder tree.
explanation: Medieval European folklore identifying the Sambucus nigra as the 'Judas tree'.

text: The rooster that crowed at Peter was named Gallus.
explanation: Medieval folk passion plays personified the rooster.

text: Barabbas was a misunderstood freedom fighter.
explanation: The Gospels plainly state Barabbas was a robber, murderer, and insurrectionist (John 18:40, Mark 15:7).

text: Pilate washed his hands in a golden basin.
explanation: Matthew 27:24 says he took water and washed his hands; the golden basin is medieval drama.

text: The crown of thorns was made of English blackberry brambles.
explanation: It was woven from Middle Eastern Ziziphus spina-christi (Christ's Thorn Jujube).

text: The cross was made of four types of wood: cedar, cypress, olive, and pine.
explanation: From the medieval Golden Legend (Legenda Aurea) by Jacobus de Voragine.

text: Longinus was the Roman soldier who pierced Jesus with the spear.
explanation: The soldier is unnamed in John 19:34; the name 'Longinus' first appears in the 4th-century Apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus.
misconception: Apocryphal name from the Gospel of Nicodemus.

text: Veronica wiped the face of Jesus with a veil.
explanation: The Sixth Station of the Cross; the story emerged in medieval Western European Catholic tradition.

text: Dismas was the name of the penitent thief.
explanation: The thieves are unnamed in the canonical Gospels; 'Dismas' comes from the apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus.

text: The holy grail was the chalice of the Last Supper.
explanation: From Chrétien de Troyes's 12th-century Arthurian romance Perceval, not the Bible.

text: Joseph of Arimathea brought the Holy Grail to Glastonbury, England.
explanation: A 13th-century legend popularized by French poet Robert de Boron.

text: The three archangels are Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael.
explanation: Michael is the only one explicitly titled 'archangel' in the Protestant Bible (Jude 1:9); Raphael appears in the deuterocanonical Book of Tobit.
misconception: Raphael is in the Book of Tobit.

text: Uriel is the fourth archangel guarding the gates of Eden.
explanation: Uriel appears in Jewish apocryphal 2 Esdras and 1 Enoch, not the canonical Bible.

text: Metatron is the highest angel in heaven.
explanation: Metatron is a prominent figure in Jewish Kabbalah and Merkabah mysticism, completely absent from the Bible.

text: Lilith was Adam's rebellious first wife before Eve.
explanation: A figure from Mesopotamian mythology and the medieval Alphabet of Ben Sira (c. 10th century); Isaiah 34:14 mentions a screech owl/night creature.

text: Belial was a fallen angel who invented heavy artillery in heaven.
explanation: From John Milton's epic Paradise Lost (Book 6).
misconception: Milton's poetic imagination in Paradise Lost.

text: Asmodeus is the demon king of vanity.
explanation: Asmodeus appears in the Book of Tobit and Talmudic legends, not canonical scripture.

text: Behemoth was a woolly mammoth.
explanation: Job 40:15-24 describes Behemoth with a tail like a cedar, unlike elephant or mammoth tails.

text: Leviathan was a fire-breathing crocodile.
explanation: Job 41 poetically portrays Leviathan as a great sea monster out of which go burning lamps and sparks.

text: The mark of Cain was black skin.
explanation: A racist 19th-century American pseudo-theological myth used to justify slavery; Genesis 4:15 gives no description of the protective mark.

text: Ham was cursed by Noah.
explanation: Genesis 9:25 explicitly says: 'Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be unto his brethren.' Noah cursed Canaan, not Ham.

text: Moses' wife Zipporah was Egyptian.
explanation: Exodus 2:16-21 states Zipporah was the daughter of Reuel, the priest of Midian (a Midianite).

text: The Queen of Sheba married Solomon and had a son named Menelik.
explanation: This is the national founding legend of Ethiopia in the 14th-century Kebra Nagast, not found in 1 Kings 10.

text: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego were thrown into a volcano.
explanation: Daniel 3:19-20 states they were cast into a burning fiery brick kiln or furnace.

text: Belshazzar was the biological son of Nebuchadnezzar.
explanation: Belshazzar was the son and coregent of Nabonidus; 'son' in Daniel 5 is used in the semitic sense of royal successor.

text: The Apostle Thomas traveled to America.
explanation: A 19th-century Mormon assertion; ancient Christian history associates Thomas with Parthia and southern India.

text: He hangeth the earth upon nothing.
explanation: Job 26:7, Job's remarkable cosmological declaration that the earth is suspended in empty space.

text: Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?
explanation: Job 38:31, God interrogating Job regarding stellar constellations.

text: Doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom, and stretch her wings toward the south?
explanation: Job 39:26, God demonstrating human ignorance of avian migratory instincts.

text: Canst thou draw out leviathan with an hook? or his tongue with a cord which thou lettest down?
explanation: Job 41:1, God confronting Job with the unconquerable sea monster.

text: I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee.
explanation: Job 42:5, Job's climax of personal repentance and intimate revelation.

text: Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes.
explanation: Job 42:6, Job's final confession before God restores him.

text: And the Lord turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends.
explanation: Job 42:10, God restoring Job when he interceded for his accusatory friends.
misconception: The turning point of Job's restoration.

text: Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts.
explanation: Psalm 42:7, poetic Hebrew imagery of overwhelming sorrow and spiritual longing.

text: My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue is the pen of a ready writer.
explanation: Psalm 45:1, royal messianic epithalamium.

text: Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre.
explanation: Psalm 45:6, quoted in Hebrews 1:8 directly addressing the Son as God.
misconception: Addressed to the divine Son in Hebrews 1:8.

text: He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass: as showers that water the earth.
explanation: Psalm 72:6, Solomonic messianic psalm of refreshing kingdom rule.

text: Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.
explanation: Psalm 73:25, Asaph's profound spiritual realization after near apostasy.

text: My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever.
explanation: Psalm 73:26, Asaph's triumph over material jealousy.

text: For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
explanation: Psalm 84:10, sons of Korah exalting the temple presence of God.

text: Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations.
explanation: Psalm 90:1, the opening line of the ancient prayer of Moses.
misconception: The only psalm attributed to Moses.

text: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
explanation: Psalm 90:12, Moses praying for perspective on life's brevity.

text: And let the beauty of the Lord our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands.
explanation: Psalm 90:17, conclusion of Moses' psalm of prayer.

text: Say among the heathen that the Lord reigneth: the world also shall be established that it shall not be moved.
explanation: Psalm 96:10, coronation psalm proclaiming Yahweh's reign.

text: Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart.
explanation: Psalm 97:11, beautiful poetic imagery of light blossoming.

text: The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.
explanation: Psalm 110:1, the most frequently quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament.
misconception: Most quoted OT verse in the NT.

text: Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.
explanation: Psalm 110:4, foundation for the Book of Hebrews' high priestly theology.

text: Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.
explanation: Psalm 116:15, solace verse regarding the passing of righteous believers.

text: I have refrained my feet from every evil way, that I might keep thy word.
explanation: Psalm 119:101, acrostic meditation on holy obedience.
misconception: From the Mem section of Psalm 119.

text: How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!
explanation: Psalm 119:103, David's sensory delight in Scripture.

text: The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
explanation: Psalm 119:130, divine illumination of God's Word.

text: Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them.
explanation: Psalm 119:165, immunity from spiritual stumbling through God's law.

text: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the Lord, which made heaven and earth.
explanation: Psalm 121:1-2, opening of the great traveler's song of ascents.

text: He will not suffer thy foot to be moved: he that keepeth thee will not slumber.
explanation: Psalm 121:3, God's sleepless vigilance over His people.

text: The sun shall not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night.
explanation: Psalm 121:6, complete day-and-night preservation.

text: The Lord shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore.
explanation: Psalm 121:8, closing benediction of Psalm 121.

text: I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the Lord.
explanation: Psalm 122:1, David's pilgrim joy arriving at Jerusalem.
misconception: Classic entrance verse for public worship.

text: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: they shall prosper that love thee.
explanation: Psalm 122:6, command to intercede for Zion's welfare.

text: They that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
explanation: Psalm 126:5, song of ascents on spiritual harvest following sorrow.
misconception: Sowing in tears, reaping in joy.

text: He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.
explanation: Psalm 126:6, classic missionary harvest verse.

text: Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O Lord.
explanation: Psalm 130:1, opening of the famous penitential De Profundis.

text: If thou, Lord, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?
explanation: Psalm 130:3, humble recognition of universal guilt before holy God.

text: But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared.
explanation: Psalm 130:4, profound theological connection between pardon and reverence.
misconception: Forgiveness producing true fear of God.

text: My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning.
explanation: Psalm 130:6, intense spiritual expectancy.

text: Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child.
explanation: Psalm 131:2, David's portrait of mature humble quietness.

text: Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?
explanation: Psalm 139:7, David marveling at God's inescapable omnipresence.

text: Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips.
explanation: Psalm 141:3, David's prayer for self-control in speech.

text: Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness: and let him reprove me; it shall be an excellent oil.
explanation: Psalm 141:5, welcoming constructive godly correction.

text: He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.
explanation: Psalm 147:3, God's tender restoration of wounded souls.
misconception: God as physician of the brokenhearted.

text: He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names.
explanation: Psalm 147:4, God naming every star in the universe.

text: Praise ye the Lord from the heavens: praise him in the heights. Praise ye him, all his angels.
explanation: Psalm 148:1-2, universal cosmic call to praise.

text: Let them praise his name in the dance: let them sing praises unto him with the timbrel and harp.
explanation: Psalm 149:3, joyful praise with instruments and sacred dance.

text: Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.
explanation: Proverbs 4:7, Solomon passing down his father David's counsel.

text: Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
explanation: Proverbs 4:23, guarding the spiritual inner spring of existence.

text: Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned?
explanation: Proverbs 6:27, warning against the self-destructive folly of adultery.

text: These six things doth the Lord hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him.
explanation: Proverbs 6:16, biblical enumeration of abominations (pride, lying, shedding innocent blood, etc.).
misconception: The biblical alternative to 'seven deadly sins'.

text: A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood.
explanation: Proverbs 6:17, the opening three items God hates in Proverbs 6.
misconception: First items on God's hate list in Proverbs.

text: Say unto wisdom, Thou art my sister; and call understanding thy kinswoman.
explanation: Proverbs 7:4, personification of wisdom as intimate family.

text: Doth not wisdom cry? and understanding put forth her voice?
explanation: Proverbs 8:1, wisdom calling aloud at the city gates.
misconception: Opening of the grand wisdom hymn in Proverbs 8.

text: The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old.
explanation: Proverbs 8:22, wisdom present before creation, prefiguring Christ.

text: When he appointed the foundations of the earth: Then I was by him, as one brought up with him.
explanation: Proverbs 8:29-30, wisdom as the master craftsman rejoicing before God.

text: Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant.
explanation: Proverbs 9:17, the alluring lie of foolishness and secret sin.

text: A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish son is the heaviness of his mother.
explanation: Proverbs 10:1, opening the main Solomonic collection.

text: Treasures of wickedness profit nothing: but righteousness delivereth from death.
explanation: Proverbs 10:2, contrast between ill-gotten gain and righteous life.

text: The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot.
explanation: Proverbs 10:7, the enduring memorial of righteous integrity.

text: He that walketh uprightly walketh surely: but he that perverteth his ways shall be known.
explanation: Proverbs 10:9, security of honesty versus exposure of deceit.

text: In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise.
explanation: Proverbs 10:19, wisdom in restraining excessive speech.

text: The blessing of the Lord, it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it.
explanation: Proverbs 10:22, true wealth coming without sorrow.

text: A false balance is abomination to the Lord: but a just weight is his delight.
explanation: Proverbs 11:1, God demanding honest business integrity.

text: When pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom.
explanation: Proverbs 11:2, pride bringing inevitable disgrace.

text: As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion.
explanation: Proverbs 11:22, vivid biblical contrast between outward beauty and missing discretion.

text: The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself.
explanation: Proverbs 11:25, generous souls flourishing.

text: He that troubleth his own house shall inherit the wind.
explanation: Proverbs 11:29, destruction of family discord.
misconception: Source of the title 'Inherit the Wind'.

text: Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish.
explanation: Proverbs 12:1, love of learning versus resisting correction.

text: A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.
explanation: Proverbs 12:10, kindness to animals as a mark of righteousness.

text: There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health.
explanation: Proverbs 12:18, destructive verbal attacks versus healing speech.

text: He that keepeth his mouth keepeth his life: but he that openeth wide his lips shall have destruction.
explanation: Proverbs 13:3, governing one's speech.

text: Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.
explanation: Proverbs 13:12, psychological truth of postponed expectation.
misconception: Hope deferred making the heart sick.

text: He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.
explanation: Proverbs 13:20, influence of friendships on character.

text: He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes.
explanation: Proverbs 13:24, the exact scriptural source misquoted as 'spare the rod, spoil the child'.
misconception: Exact source of the misquoted proverb.

text: Every wise woman buildeth her house: but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands.
explanation: Proverbs 14:1, wise homemaking versus self-destructive folly.

text: There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.
explanation: Proverbs 14:12 and 16:25, solemn warning against subjective moral self-deception.

text: The heart knoweth his own bitterness; and a stranger doth not intermeddle with his joy.
explanation: Proverbs 14:10, the deep private interior world of each human soul.

text: In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.
explanation: Proverbs 14:23, value of diligent work over empty talking.

text: He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly.
explanation: Proverbs 14:29, patience indicating emotional maturity.

text: The eyes of the Lord are in every place, beholding the evil and the good.
explanation: Proverbs 15:3, divine omniscience observing all human conduct.
